source_text: δεκάτωσις τῷ κυρίῳ, γενικῶς ἐπινενόηται–»ὅτε συνήντησεν αὐτῷ» –τουτέστιν τῷ Ἀβραάμ–»ὁ Μελχισεδέκ». 15.81 Τί δὴ οὖν τὸ βούλημα τῆς κενολογίας αὐτῶν καὶ πῇ τὸ ἄτοπον; σύνες γάρ· ὅσοι ἐθέλωσι λέγειν ἀρχήν, καὶ πέρας ὁμολογοῦσιν, καὶ τῷ γένεσιν ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι, καὶ τὴν ἐκ ταύτης θνῆσιν ἀποδέχονται· 15.82 καὶ τῷ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἢ ἐξ ἀνομοίας τῆς θεϊκῆς οὐσίας ὑπολαμβάνειν γεγενῆσθαι, θνητόν τε ἅμα καὶ ἀλλότριον τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς συνθεότητος ἀποφαίνονται, ὅπερ καὶ λεγόμενον μόνον, οὐχὶ καὶ δοξαζόμενον πάσης ἀθεΐας ἀνάμεστον. 15.83 Ἀλλὰ πρὸς τό «ἐν ἀρχῇ 12 ἦν ὁ λόγος» τὰ ἐκείνων δῆθεν ἰσχυρά; ἐγράφη καὶ περὶ τῆς κτίσεως, φησίν, τό «ἦν». ἔχει γάρ «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν, ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος», καί «ἦν ἄνθρωπος ἐξ Ἀρμαθὲμ Σιφά». 15.84 Οὐδὲν δὲ κοινὸν τῷ «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν» καὶ τῷ «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν», οὐδὲ τῷ κτίστῃ πρὸς τὸ κτίσμα. τὸ γάρ «ἦν» ἐπὶ τῆς κτίσεως περὶ μόνου τοῦ ῥέοντος χρόνου τοῦ καὶ περατουμένου λέγεται καὶ πιστεύεται. 15.85 Ἦν γὰρ ἡ κτίσις μετὰ τὸ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι. εἶπεν γὰρ προλαβὼν ὅτι ἐποίησεν αὐτήν, καὶ τότε ἐπήγαγεν τό «ἦν», ἵνα μὴ αὐτόματος νομισθῇ. 15.86 Ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου τὸ ὑπεράναρχον σημαίνει. «ἐν ἀρχῇ» γάρ, φησίν, «ἦν» καί «θεὸς ἦν», καὶ τό «ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν» τὸ ἐκ μὴ ὄντων ἐξωθεῖ. 15.87 Μαρτυροῦσι δὲ περὶ μὲν τοῦ εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν προαιώνιον καὶ ποιητὴν τῶν αἰώνων ὧδε· Παῦλος ἐπιστέλλων Ἑβραίοις μέν· «πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως πάλαι ὁ θεὸς λαλήσας τοῖς πατράσιν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις ἐπ' ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ, ὃν ἔθη κεν κληρονόμον πάντων, δι' οὗ καὶ τοὺς αἰῶνας ἐποίησεν». αὐτὸς οὖν τὰ ἑαυτοῦ κληρονομεῖ καὶ ὡς ποιητὴς αὐτῶν καὶ ὡς ἀληθινὸς υἱός· ἐτέθη δὲ κληρονόμος ὡς ἐνανθρωπήσας. 15.88 Κορινθίοις δὲ ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ ἐπιστολῇ· «θεμέλιον γὰρ οὐδεὶς δύναται θεῖναι παρὰ τὸν κείμενον, ὅς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός», τουτέστιν, ἀρχὴν ἐπινοηθῆναι τοῦ υἱοῦ ἀμήχανον. «ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ» πᾶσα ἀρχή. 15.89 ∆αυῒδ δὲ ἐν ογʹ ψαλμῷ περὶ τοῦ ἀνάρχου ψάλλων· «ὁ δὲ θεὸς βασιλεὺς ἡμῶν προαιώνιος εἰργάσατο σωτηρίαν ἐν μέσῳ τῆς γῆς». λέγει δὲ τὸν Γολγοθᾶν, τόπον μεσώτατον καὶ οἱονεὶ κέντρον τῆς ὑπ' οὐρανὸν ὀνομάζων αὐτόν· ἐν ᾧ τῇ μὲν θεϊκῇ αὐτοῦ προγνώσει πρὸ αἰῶνος εἰργάσατο ἡμῖν σωτηρίαν ἐν τῇ ἐνανθρωπήσει ὁ υἱός, τῷ δὲ πράγματι, ὅτε δι' ἀγαθότητα ἔπαθεν ὡς οἶδεν καὶ ἠθέλησεν ὁ ἀπαθὴς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν καὶ ἕως «τῆς καρδίας τῆς γῆς», ὡς εἰπεῖν, ἐγένετο, καθὰ καὶ Ἰεζεκιὴλ προφητεύει τοιάδε· «αὐτὴν Ἱερουσαλήμ, εἰς μέσον τῶν ἐθνῶν τέθεικα αὐτήν». 15.90 Καὶ ἐν ριηʹ ψαλμῷ· «εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, κύριε, ὁ λόγος σου διαμένει ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ». καὶ αὐτὸς περὶ ἑαυτοῦ ὁ δεσπότης αἱρετικοῖς που πάντως ἀποκλείων εἶπεν· «ἀμήν, ἀμήν, λέγω σοι, πρό» τοῦ τοὺς αἰῶνας γενέσθαι «ἐγώ εἰμι». 15.91 Περὶ δὲ τοῦ καθεστάναι πάντων ἀσωμάτων τε καὶ σωματοειδῶν δημιουργόν, οὐχὶ δὲ ὑπουργὸν ἢ μεσίτην, ἐν ταὐτῷ δὲ καὶ ἄναρχον, πρὸς ταῖς ἤδη παρατεθείσαις μαρτυρίαις καὶ ∆αυῒδ ἐν ριγʹ ψαλμῷ ᾄδει· «ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ πάντα ὅσα ἠθέλησεν ἐποίησεν». οὐκ εἶπεν· «ὅσα ἐπετράπη». 15.92 τίς οὖν καταρνήσαιτ' ἂν τῆς αὐτεξουσίου καὶ παντεξουσίου μονάδος οὐσίας ὑπάρχειν τὸν ἐθελουσίως αὐτουργοῦντα καὶ ἔχοντα ψιλῷ τῷ οἰκείῳ νεύματι πάντα δίχα μελλήσεως συντρέχοντα; 15.93 Καὶ ἐν ραʹ ψαλμῷ· «κατ' ἀρχὰς τὴν γῆν σύ, κύριε, ἐθεμελίωσας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σού εἰσιν οἱ οὐρανοί. αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμενεῖς. καὶ πάντες ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιωθήσονται, καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον εἱλίξεις αὐτούς, καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται. σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ, καὶ τὰ ἔτη σου οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν», ἀντὶ τοῦ «ἄναρχος ὑπάρχεις καὶ ἀπέραντος.» 15.94 Καὶ Παῦλος δὲ τὰ ἴσα γράφει πρὸς Ἐφεσίους μέν· «ἐν τῷ θεῷ τῷ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι», πρὸς δὲ Κολοσσαεῖς· «ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα, τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὁρατὰ καὶ ἀόρατα, εἴτε θρόνοι εἴτε κυριότητες εἴτε ἀρχαὶ εἴτε ἐξουσίαι· τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἐκτίσθη, καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων, καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκεν». 15.95 τοῦ γὰρ οὐσιωδῶς ἐξεικονίζοντος τὸν θεὸν καὶ τοῦ πρὸ πάντων τῇ θεότητι οὐδεὶς ὑπέρκειται οὐδὲ πρεσβυτερεύει, ὡς τοῦ μετὰ πάντας οὐδεὶς ὑπόκειται οὐδὲ ὑστερεύει. 15.96 Καὶ ἄλλως· εἰ πρὸ πάντων ἐστὶν μόνος ἐκ μόνου καὶ μόνως, πρὸ πάσης ἐνεργείας ἀπορρήτως ἐγεννήθη καὶ οὐσιωδῶς υἱός ἐστι τοῦ πατρός. δεῖ γὰρ
pass_a_gloss: [15.80 continued from the previous section: 'Levi, the descendant of Abraham, from whom the'] tithing to the Lord, has been conceived generically: 'when he met him' (that is, Abraham) 'Melchizedek'. 15.81 What then is the intent of their empty talk, and in what [lies] the absurdity? Understand: as many as wish to speak of a beginning also confess an end, and by professing a coming-to-be also accept the dying out of this. 15.82 And by supposing [him] to have come to be out of things not being or out of unlikeness of the divine substance, they declare [him] at the same time mortal and alien to the co-Godhead of the Father, which, even only being said, not also being held as opinion, is filled full of all godlessness. 15.83 But against 'in the beginning was the Word' [what are] their supposedly strong [points]? The 'was' was written also about the creation, he says. For it has: 'in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth, and the earth was unseen and unfurnished', and 'there was a man from Armathaim Sipha'. 15.84 But nothing [is] common to 'in the beginning was' and to 'in the beginning he made', nor to the creator toward the creature. For the 'was' in the case of the creation is said and believed about the flowing and ending time alone. 15.85 For the creation was after coming to be out of things not being. For having said beforehand that he made it, then also he brought on the 'was', so that it would not be thought self-made. 15.86 But in the case of God the Word it signifies the beyond-beginningless. For 'in the beginning', he says, 'was', and 'was God', and the 'in the beginning was' pushes out the 'out of things not being'. 15.87 And they testify concerning the Son's being before the ages and maker of the ages thus: Paul sending a letter to Hebrews: 'in many parts and many ways of old God, having spoken to the fathers in the prophets, at the last of these days spoke to us in a Son, whom he set heir of all, through whom also he made the ages'. He himself then inherits the things of himself, both as their maker and as true Son; and he was set heir as having become man. 15.88 And to Corinthians in the first letter: 'for a foundation no one can lay beside the one lying, who is Jesus Christ', that is, [it is] without means that a beginning of the Son be conceived. For 'in him and through him' [is] every beginning. 15.89 And David in the seventy-third [Greek numbering] psalm, singing about the beginningless one: 'and God our king before the ages worked salvation in the middle of the earth'. And he speaks of Golgotha, naming it a most middle place and as it were a centre of the [land] under heaven; in which by his divine foreknowledge before an age the Son worked salvation for us in the becoming-man, and in the deed, when through goodness he suffered, as he knew and willed, the impassible one, on our behalf, and came even up to 'the heart of the earth', so to say, according as also Ezekiel prophesies such things: 'Jerusalem herself, into the middle of the nations I have set her'. 15.90 And in the hundred and eighteenth [Greek numbering] psalm: 'into the age, Lord, your word remains in the heaven'. And the master himself, about himself, surely shutting off heretics somewhere, said: 'amen, amen, I say to you, before' the ages came to be 'I am'. 15.91 And concerning his having been established craftsman of all bodiless and body-formed things, and not an under-worker or a mediator, and in the same [respect] also beginningless, in addition to the testimonies already set beside, also David in the hundred and thirteenth [Greek numbering] psalm sings: 'our God in the heaven and in the earth made all things as many as he willed'. He did not say: 'as many as he was charged with'. 15.92 Who then would deny that the one working by himself willingly and having all things running together by his own bare nod without delay is of the self-authoritative and all-authoritative substance of the Monad? 15.93 And in the hundred and first [Greek numbering] psalm: 'at the beginnings you, Lord, founded the earth, and works of your hands are the heavens. They will perish, but you will remain; and all will grow old like a garment, and like a wrap you will roll them, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not give out', in place of 'you exist beginningless and boundless'. 15.94 And Paul also writes the equal things, to Ephesians: 'in the God who created all things', and to Colossians: 'because in him were created all things, those in the heavens and those upon the earth, seen and unseen, whether thrones or lordships or rules or authorities; all things were created through him and into him, and he is before all things, and all things stand together in him'. 15.95 For over the one substantially imaging God and the one before all in Godhead no one lies above nor is elder, as under the one after all no one lies beneath nor comes behind. 15.96 And otherwise: if he is before all things, alone from alone and alone-wise, before every activity he was begotten unspeakably and is substantially Son of the Father. For it is necessary [breaks off; continued in the next unit]
pass_b_english: … tithing for the Lord comes, is meant in a general sense: “when Melchizedek met him” (Hebrews 7:10), that is, met Abraham.

What, then, is the aim of their empty talk, and where does its absurdity lie? Consider: all who wish to speak of a beginning for him confess an end as well; and by declaring that he came into being, they also accept the death that follows from coming into being. And by supposing that he came to be from things that are not, or from a substance unlike the divine one, they declare him at once mortal and a stranger to the Godhead he shares with the Father. Even to say this, let alone to believe it, is full of every kind of godlessness.

But what are their supposedly strong arguments against “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1)? “The word ‘was’,” he says, “was written of creation too. For Scripture has, ‘In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth; and the earth was invisible and unformed’ (Genesis 1:1-2), and ‘There was a man from Armathaim Sipha’ (1 Samuel 1:1).”

But “In the beginning was” has nothing in common with “In the beginning he made,” any more than the Creator has with the creature. For “was,” in the case of creation, is said and believed only of time, which flows and comes to an end. Creation “was” after it came to be from things that are not. Scripture first said that God made it, and only then added “was,” so that it would not be thought to have come about of itself. But in the case of God the Word, “was” signifies what is beyond all beginning. For “In the beginning,” it says, “was,” and “was God” (John 1:1); and “In the beginning was” drives out “from things that are not.”

That the Son is before the ages and the Maker of the ages, the witnesses testify thus. Paul, writing to the Hebrews: “In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (Hebrews 1:1-2). So he inherits what is his own, both as its Maker and as true Son; and he was appointed heir as having become man. And to the Corinthians, in the first letter: “For no one can lay a foundation other than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11); that is, it is impossible to conceive a beginning of the Son. For “in him and through him” (Colossians 1:16) is every beginning.

And David in the seventy-fourth Psalm, singing of the one without beginning: “But God, our King before the ages, worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 74:12). He means Golgotha, calling it the most central place and, as it were, the centre of the land under heaven. There the Son worked salvation for us in his becoming man: by his divine foreknowledge before the age, and in deed when he, the impassible one, suffered for us out of goodness, as he knew and willed, and came, so to speak, even to “the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). So Ezekiel too prophesies: “Jerusalem herself, I have set her in the midst of the nations” (Ezekiel 5:5).

And in the hundred and nineteenth Psalm: “For ever, Lord, your word endures in heaven” (Psalm 119:89). And the Master himself, speaking of himself, surely shutting the door on heretics, said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, before” the ages came to be, “I am” (John 8:58).

As for his being established as the Maker of all things, bodiless and bodily, not an assistant or a go-between, and at the same time without beginning: besides the testimonies already set out, David also sings in the hundred and fifteenth Psalm, “Our God in heaven and on earth has done all things whatever he willed” (Psalm 115:3). He did not say “whatever he was assigned.” Who then would deny that he who works by himself, of his own will, and has all things running together at his bare nod without delay, belongs to the self-governing and all-governing substance of the Monad?

And in the hundred and second Psalm: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain; and all of them will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:25-27), meaning, “You are without beginning and without end.”

Paul too writes the same, to the Ephesians, “in God who created all things” (Ephesians 3:9), and to the Colossians, “For in him all things were created, in the heavens and on the earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities; all things were created through him and for him, and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16-17). For above him who images God in his very being and is before all things in Godhead no one is set and no one is older, just as below the one who comes after all no one is set and no one is later.

Put another way: if he is before all things, alone from the Alone and in a manner his alone, he was begotten ineffably before every activity and is the Son of the Father in his very being. For it is necessary …

choices.issue: Old draft garbled, wrong Psalm numbers and references
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English turned the opening into 'The meeting with the Lord was thought of generally… the Melchizedek'; made 15.81-15.82 'promise to the generation', 'foreign to the composition of the Father' and 'not even honored, as a mediator of all ungodliness'; rendered τὸ ὑπεράναρχον as 'the super-beginning' and ἐξωθεῖ as 'pushes out from non-existence'; read ἀνάρχου as 'the ruler'; split 15.89 into a fragment paragraph ('A center which names him under heaven'); made 15.91 a sentence without a main verb; read νεύματι (nod) as 'breath', μελλήσεως (delay) as 'necessity' and ὑπάρχειν as 'exists'; read ἀπορρήτως (ineffably) as 'absolutely' and μόνως as 'by alone'; and used bracket fillers '[Him]', '[generation]'. Psalm numbers: '84th' corrected to seventy-fourth (LXX 73), '33rd' to hundred and fifteenth (LXX 113), '89th' to hundred and second (LXX 101). References: Ezekiel 28:26 corrected to Ezekiel 5:5; Psalm 102:25 widened to 102:25-27; '(Gen 1:1-2)', '(Heb 1:1-2)', '(1 Cor 3:11)' written out; Hebrews 7:10, Colossians 1:16 and Matthew 12:40 added.

choices.english: … tithing for the Lord comes, is meant in a general sense
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence: u03-rem-mid ends 'Levi, the descendant of Abraham, from whom the …' (παρ' οὗ ἡ). Didymus explains that 'Levi' in Hebrews 7:9-10 stands generally for the tithe-receiving line. 'comes' is the least verb English needs for 'from whom the tithing'.

choices.term: ὅτε συνήντησεν αὐτῷ –τουτέστιν τῷ Ἀβραάμ– ὁ Μελχισεδέκ
choices.english: “when Melchizedek met him” (Hebrews 7:10), that is, met Abraham
choices.why: Didymus sets his gloss inside the quotation; English moves it after the quoted words.
δοξάζω here is 'hold an opinion', not 'honour'; the old 'not even honored' misread it.

choices.english: from a substance unlike the divine one
choices.why: The Anomoean claim (the Son unlike the Father in substance).

choices.english: “The word ‘was’,” he says, “was written of creation too …”
choices.why: φησίν gives the opponents' objection in their own voice, so it is printed as their speech.
Didymus' LXX form of the place name (1 Kingdoms 1:1), not the Hebrew 'Ramathaim-zophim'.
Stronger than ἄναρχος: the Word does not merely lack a beginning, he is beyond the category.

choices.term: ἐν ογʹ / ριηʹ / ριγʹ / ραʹ ψαλμῷ
choices.english: seventy-fourth / hundred and nineteenth / hundred and fifteenth / hundred and second Psalm
choices.why: Greek (LXX) numbers 73, 118, 113, 101 converted to English numbering; LXX 113 covers English Psalms 114-115, and the verse quoted is Psalm 115:3.
Didymus' wording; the LXX of Ezekiel 5:5 has αὕτη ('this is Jerusalem').

choices.english: “before” the ages came to be, “I am”
choices.why: The copy-text quotes only 'before' and 'I am' from John 8:58; Didymus puts 'the ages came to be' where the Gospel has 'Abraham was'. The quotation marks follow the copy-text.
Didymus denies that the Son is a subordinate agent of creation; 'mediator' is avoided because of its other New Testament sense.
ἐπιτρέπω here 'be charged, commissioned': the point is that the Son acts by his own will, not under orders.

choices.term: τῆς αὐτεξουσίου καὶ παντεξουσίου μονάδος οὐσίας ὑπάρχειν
choices.english: belongs to the self-governing and all-governing substance of the Monad
choices.why: ὑπάρχειν with the genitive is 'to be of, belong to'; the old 'exists' lost the construction.

choices.english: alone from the Alone and in a manner his alone
choices.why: Keeps Didymus' triple play on μόνος.
The printed line number '12' in 15.83 is page debris, skipped; ἔθη κεν is one word split by a line break.
